The Discrete Monotonicity Property in Rank Two

Fei Xue Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing 210046, China Email address: 05429@njnu.edu.cn
Date: October 28, 2026
Abstract.

The Betke–Henk–Wills conjecture predicts a bound for lattice-point counts in terms of successive minima. Malikiosis introduced the discrete monotonicity property for normalized residue counts as a sufficient condition for this bound and its extension to nonsymmetric convex bodies. We prove that every compact convex set satisfies this property for lattice subgroups of rank at most two, in arbitrary ambient dimension.

Key words and phrases: 
discrete monotonicity, lattice-convex sets, residue classes, finite tori, successive minima
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11H06, 52C05; Secondary 52C07, 05A20

1. Introduction

For an oo-symmetric convex body C=−C⊆ℝdC=-C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and a full-rank lattice Λ\Lambda, the jjth successive minimum λj​(C,Λ)\lambda_{j}(C,\Lambda) is the least λ>0\lambda>0 for which λ​C\lambda C contains jj linearly independent vectors of Λ\Lambda. For an arbitrary convex body K⊆ℝdK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, Malikiosis’s extension of the Betke–Henk–Wills conjecture asserts that

(1.1) #⁡(K∩Λ)≤∏j=1d(⌊2λj​((K−K)/2,Λ)⌋+1).\#(K\cap\Lambda)\leq\prod_{j=1}^{d}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2}{\lambda_{j}\bigl((K-K)/2,\Lambda\bigr)}\right\rfloor+1\right).

For K=−KK=-K, this is the original conjecture of Betke, Henk, and Wills [5, Conjecture 2.1], who proved it in dimension two [5, Theorem 2.2]. Malikiosis proved (1.1) in dimensions at most three [6, Corollary 4.1.1]. Tointon [7] obtained improved bounds in general dimension.

Malikiosis introduced a discrete monotonicity property that compares normalized residue counts at different moduli. His criterion for (1.1) uses only subgroups of rank below the ambient dimension [6, proof of Theorem 4.2.1], so our rank-two result recovers the known three-dimensional bound. For a compact convex set K⊆ℝdK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, a lattice Λ⊆ℝd\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, and a subgroup Γ≤Λ\Gamma\leq\Lambda, write

(1.2) DΛ​(K,r​Γ):=#⁡{x+r​Γ:x∈K∩Λ}(r∈ℤ>0).D_{\Lambda}(K,r\Gamma):=\#\{x+r\Gamma:x\in K\cap\Lambda\}\qquad(r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}).

Thus DΛ​(K,r​Γ)D_{\Lambda}(K,r\Gamma) counts the cosets of r​Γr\Gamma containing a lattice point of KK. The set KK has the discrete monotonicity property with respect to Λ\Lambda if

(1.3) r⟼DΛ​(K,r​Γ)rrank⁡Γr\longmapsto\frac{D_{\Lambda}(K,r\Gamma)}{r^{\rank\Gamma}}

is nonincreasing on the positive integers for every subgroup Γ≤Λ\Gamma\leq\Lambda [6, Definition 4.2.1]. This is a discrete counterpart of the quotient-volume monotonicity in classical proofs of Minkowski’s second theorem [2].

Theorem 1.1 (Rank-two discrete monotonicity).

Let K⊆ℝdK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be compact and convex, let Λ⊆ℝd\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be a lattice, and let Γ≤Λ\Gamma\leq\Lambda have rank i≤2i\leq 2. Then

(1.4) DΛ​(K,r​Γ)ri≥DΛ​(K,s​Γ)si\frac{D_{\Lambda}(K,r\Gamma)}{r^{i}}\geq\frac{D_{\Lambda}(K,s\Gamma)}{s^{i}}

for all positive integers r≤sr\leq s.

By the reductions and initial cases in Section 2, it suffices to compare moduli rr and r+1r+1 for planar lattice-convex sets. We first choose a lattice-convex subset containing exactly one point from each represented class at the larger modulus (Lemma 3.1). A suitable lattice basis then places the points of each class at the smaller modulus among four corners of a lattice parallelogram (Corollary 3.3). Unless all classes at the smaller modulus are represented, we select lattice segments whose number equals the difference between the residue counts at moduli r+1r+1 and rr. Their residue images are distinct lines in at most three directions (Section 4). By Proposition 5.1, these lines are contained in a cover of the finite torus with 2​r+1=(r+1)2−r22r+1=(r+1)^{2}-r^{2} lines. Lemma 5.2 bounds the number of points covered by the selected lines, proving the comparison from rr to r+1r+1.

2. Preliminaries

Throughout, a lattice has full rank in its real span. For a finite subset AA of a lattice LL, put

(2.1) Nr​(A,L):=#⁡{a+r​L:a∈A}(r∈ℤ>0).N_{r}(A;L):=\#\{a+rL:a\in A\}\qquad(r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}).

This is the number of distinct cosets of r​LrL meeting AA. We omit LL when the ambient lattice is fixed. We call AA lattice-convex if A=conv⁡(A)∩LA=\conv(A)\cap L. If A=K∩LA=K\cap L is nonempty and P=conv⁡(A)P=\conv(A), then P⊆KP\subseteq K and P∩L=AP\cap L=A. Thus residue counts for compact convex sets reduce to those for finite lattice-convex sets. If A=∅A=\varnothing, all residue counts are zero.

A nonzero vector of LL is primitive if it is not an integer multiple k​vkv with v∈Lv\in L and k≥2k\geq 2.

Lemma 2.1 (Affine-coset reduction).

Let K⊆ℝdK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be compact and convex, let Λ⊆ℝd\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be a lattice, and let Γ≤Λ\Gamma\leq\Lambda. For each coset ξ∈Λ/Γ\xi\in\Lambda/\Gamma, choose zξ∈ξz_{\xi}\in\xi and put

Aξ:=(K∩ξ)−zξ⊆Γ.A_{\xi}:=(K\cap\xi)-z_{\xi}\subseteq\Gamma.

Every nonempty AξA_{\xi} is lattice-convex in Γ\Gamma, only finitely many are nonempty, and

(2.2) DΛ​(K,r​Γ)=∑ξ∈Λ/ΓNr​(Aξ,Γ)(r∈ℤ>0).D_{\Lambda}(K,r\Gamma)=\sum_{\xi\in\Lambda/\Gamma}N_{r}(A_{\xi};\Gamma)\qquad(r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}).
Proof.

Congruence modulo r​Γr\Gamma never identifies points in different Γ\Gamma-cosets, which gives (2.2). Moreover, conv⁡(Aξ)+zξ⊆K\conv(A_{\xi})+z_{\xi}\subseteq K, so Γ∩conv⁡(Aξ)=Aξ\Gamma\cap\conv(A_{\xi})=A_{\xi}. Changing zξz_{\xi} translates AξA_{\xi} by an element of Γ\Gamma and preserves its residue counts. Finiteness follows from the compactness of KK and the discreteness of Λ\Lambda. ∎

It suffices to compare consecutive moduli. For a nonempty set in rank ii, N1​(A)=1N_{1}(A)=1 and N2​(A)≤2iN_{2}(A)\leq 2^{i}, so 1→21\to 2 is immediate.

Lemma 2.2 (Line formula).

Let LL have rank i≥1i\geq 1, and let A=conv⁡(A)∩LA=\conv(A)\cap L be a nonempty finite set of affine dimension at most one. If n=|A|n=|A|, then

Nq​(A,L)=min⁡(n,q)(q∈ℤ>0).N_{q}(A;L)=\min(n,q)\qquad(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}).

Consequently, Nq​(A,L)/qiN_{q}(A;L)/q^{i} is nonincreasing in qq.

Proof.

The formula is immediate for a singleton. Otherwise, translate one point of AA to the origin and put H=linℝ⁡(A−A)H=\lin_{\mathbb{R}}(A-A) and LH=L∩HL_{H}=L\cap H. The set AA consists of nn consecutive points of the rank-one lattice LHL_{H}. Since

q​L∩H=q⁡(L∩H)=q​LH,qL\cap H=q(L\cap H)=qL_{H},

congruence on AA modulo q​LqL is the same as congruence modulo q​LHqL_{H}. This proves the formula. Finally,

min⁡(n,q)qi=q1−i​min⁡{n/q,1}\frac{\min(n,q)}{q^{i}}=q^{1-i}\min\{n/q,1\}

is a product of two nonnegative nonincreasing functions. ∎

Together with Lemma 2.1, this proves the rank-one case of Theorem 1.1 and handles planar sets of affine dimension at most one. For rank zero, the residue count is independent of the modulus.

We next prove the comparison from modulus 22 to modulus 33. The argument turns a missing parity class into three missing classes modulo 3​L3L.

Proposition 2.3 (Full-lattice base step).

Let A=conv⁡(A)∩LA=\conv(A)\cap L be a finite lattice-convex set in a rank-two lattice. Then

N2​(A)4≥N3​(A)9.\frac{N_{2}(A)}{4}\geq\frac{N_{3}(A)}{9}.
Proof.

The empty case is immediate, and Lemma 2.2 handles sets of affine dimension at most one. Suppose that P=conv⁡(A)P=\conv(A) is two-dimensional. A triangle of least positive area with vertices in AA has no other lattice points. By Pick’s theorem, its two edge vectors at a vertex form a basis of LL, so N2​(A)≥3N_{2}(A)\geq 3. The case N2​(A)=4N_{2}(A)=4 is immediate. It remains to show that

(2.3) N2​(A)=3⟹N3​(A)≤6.N_{2}(A)=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_{3}(A)\leq 6.

Choose a missing class u+2​Lu+2L and put Q=(P−u)/2Q=(P-u)/2. Since QQ is compact and disjoint from LL, slightly enlarge it without meeting LL and extend the enlarged set to a maximal lattice-free convex set MM. Thus Q⊂int⁡MQ\subset\operatorname{int}M and int⁡M∩L=∅\operatorname{int}M\cap L=\varnothing. By [4, Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 2.2], MM is a strip with lattice boundary lines or a bounded polygon with a lattice point in the relative interior of every edge.

Choose z1,z2,z3∈∂M∩Lz_{1},z_{2},z_{3}\in\partial M\cap L distinct modulo 3​L3L as follows. For a strip, take three consecutive lattice points on one boundary line. For a polygon, take lattice points in the relative interiors of three different edges. In the polygon case, a congruence zi≡zj(mod3​L)z_{i}\equiv z_{j}\pmod{3L} with i≠ji\neq j would give

2​zi+zj3∈int⁡M∩L,\frac{2z_{i}+z_{j}}{3}\in\operatorname{int}M\cap L,

a contradiction.

If p∈P∩(u+2​zi+3​L)p\in P\cap(u+2z_{i}+3L), then

p−u+zi3=23​p−u2+13​zi∈int⁡M∩L,\frac{p-u+z_{i}}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{p-u}{2}+\frac{1}{3}z_{i}\in\operatorname{int}M\cap L,

a contradiction. Thus PP misses the three distinct classes u+2​zi+3​Lu+2z_{i}+3L, and N3​(A)≤6N_{3}(A)\leq 6. ∎

3. Residue representatives and lattice boxes

We work in a rank-two lattice LL and write Nq​(A)N_{q}(A) for Nq​(A,L)N_{q}(A;L). For x∈Lx\in L and primitive v∈Lv\in L, the segment [x,x+m​v][x,x+mv], m∈ℤ≥0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, has lattice length mm.

Our aim is to compare rr and s=r+1s=r+1. We first replace AA by a lattice-convex subset containing exactly one point in each class represented modulo s​LsL.

Lemma 3.1 (Residue-preserving reduction).

Let LL be a rank-two lattice, let A=conv⁡(A)∩LA=\conv(A)\cap L be finite and nonempty, and let ss be a positive integer. There is a lattice-convex set B⊆AB\subseteq A such that

(3.1) |B|=Ns​(B)=Ns​(A).\lvert B\rvert=N_{s}(B)=N_{s}(A).
Proof.

Suppose that two points of AA differ by s​u≠0su\neq 0, and let vv be the primitive direction of uu. The polygon P=conv⁡(A)P=\conv(A) has a chord of lattice length at least ss in direction vv. If PP is a segment, choose an endpoint zz from which PP contains ss primitive steps in direction vv. Otherwise, the longest-chord lemma of Bárány and Füredi [3, Lemma 1] supplies a longest chord in this primitive direction having a lattice vertex zz of PP as one endpoint. Orient vv into the chord. Then z,z+s​v∈Az,z+sv\in A.

Delete zz. Since zz is a vertex,

A∖{z}=conv⁡(A∖{z})∩L,A\setminus\{z\}=\conv(A\setminus\{z\})\cap L,

so lattice convexity is preserved. The class of zz modulo s​LsL remains represented by z+s​vz+sv. Replace PP by the convex hull of the current set and iterate. Each deletion removes one point, so the process terminates with reduction modulo s​LsL injective, giving (3.1). ∎

Since B⊆AB\subseteq A, we also have Nr​(B)≤Nr​(A)N_{r}(B)\leq N_{r}(A) for every rr. Thus a comparison for BB transfers to AA:

Nr​(A)r2≥Nr​(B)r2≥Ns​(B)s2=Ns​(A)s2.\frac{N_{r}(A)}{r^{2}}\geq\frac{N_{r}(B)}{r^{2}}\geq\frac{N_{s}(B)}{s^{2}}=\frac{N_{s}(A)}{s^{2}}.

For the adjacent comparison, let s=r+1s=r+1 and suppose that AA is injective modulo s​LsL. Put

(3.2) t:=|A|−Nr​(A)=Ns​(A)−Nr​(A).t:=\lvert A\rvert-N_{r}(A)=N_{s}(A)-N_{r}(A).

Since s2−r2=2​r+1s^{2}-r^{2}=2r+1, the adjacent comparison is equivalent to

(3.3) (2​r+1)​Nr​(A)≥r2​t.(2r+1)N_{r}(A)\geq r^{2}t.

We next place AA in a lattice box. For s=r+1s=r+1, this gives the four-corner description of the fibers modulo r​LrL in Corollary 3.3.

Lemma 3.2 (Lattice-box containment).

Let ss be a positive integer, let LL be a rank-two lattice, and let PP be a two-dimensional lattice polygon. Suppose that P∩LP\cap L is injective modulo s​LsL. There are z∈Lz\in L, a basis e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} of LL, and nonnegative integers m1,m2m_{1},m_{2} such that

(3.4) P⊆z+[0,m1]​e1+[0,m2]​e2,mi≤⌊3​s−12⌋.P\subseteq z+[0,m_{1}]e_{1}+[0,m_{2}]e_{2},\qquad m_{i}\leq\left\lfloor\frac{3s-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
Proof.

For a linear form f:linℝ⁡L→ℝf:\lin_{\mathbb{R}}L\to\mathbb{R} with f⁡(L)⊆ℤf(L)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}, put

w⁡(f)=maxx∈P⁡f⁡(x)−minx∈P⁡f⁡(x).w(f)=\max_{x\in P}f(x)-\min_{x\in P}f(x).

The longest-chord argument in Lemma 3.1 gives

(3.5) λ1​(P−P,L)>1s.\lambda_{1}(P-P,L)>\frac{1}{s}.

The planar transference inequality of Ambro and Ito [1, Theorem 6.4] therefore gives two linearly independent forms f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} satisfying w⁡(fi)<3​s/2w(f_{i})<3s/2.

Fix a basis of LL and compute determinants using the coefficient vectors of the forms in this basis. Among the independent pairs satisfying the width bounds, choose f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} to minimize the positive integer Δ=|det(f1,f2)|\Delta=|\det(f_{1},f_{2})|. If Δ>1\Delta>1, the centered parallelogram spanned by f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} contains a nonzero form gg taking integer values on LL, with

g=α​f1+β​f2,|α|,|β|≤12.g=\alpha f_{1}+\beta f_{2},\qquad|\alpha|,|\beta|\leq\frac{1}{2}.

Then

w⁡(g)≤|α|w⁡(f1)+|β|​w​(f2)<3​s/2.w(g)\leq|\alpha|w(f_{1})+|\beta|w(f_{2})<3s/2.

Moreover,

|det(f1,g)|=|β|​Δ,|det(g,f2)|=|α|​Δ.|\det(f_{1},g)|=|\beta|\Delta,\qquad|\det(g,f_{2})|=|\alpha|\Delta.

Since g≠0g\neq 0, at least one of the pairs (f1,g)(f_{1},g) and (g,f2)(g,f_{2}) is independent. This pair satisfies the width bounds and has absolute determinant at most Δ/2<Δ\Delta/2<\Delta, contradicting the choice of f1,f2f_{1},f_{2}. Thus Δ=1\Delta=1, and the vectors dual to f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} form a basis e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} of LL.

Put ai=minx∈P⁡fi​(x)a_{i}=\min_{x\in P}f_{i}(x) and mi=w⁡(fi)m_{i}=w(f_{i}). These are integers, since the extrema occur at lattice vertices. For z=a1​e1+a2​e2z=a_{1}e_{1}+a_{2}e_{2}, we obtain P⊆z+[0,m1]​e1+[0,m2]​e2P\subseteq z+[0,m_{1}]e_{1}+[0,m_{2}]e_{2} and mi<3​s/2m_{i}<3s/2, which gives (3.4). ∎

For r≥3r\geq 3 and s=r+1s=r+1, the bound in (3.4) is at most 2​r−12r-1. We use the basis supplied by Lemma 3.2. Inside this box, the points of a fixed residue class modulo r​LrL have at most two values in either coordinate, separated by rr. They therefore lie among the four corners of a translate of [0,r]​e1+[0,r]​e2[0,r]e_{1}+[0,r]e_{2}.

Corollary 3.3 (Four-corner fibers).

Let r≥3r\geq 3, let s=r+1s=r+1, and let PP be a two-dimensional lattice polygon in a rank-two lattice LL. Suppose that A=P∩LA=P\cap L is injective modulo s​LsL. In the basis of Lemma 3.2, every fiber F=A∩(a+r​L)F=A\cap(a+rL) has at most four points, and for each such FF there is a bF∈Lb_{F}\in L such that

(3.6) F−bF⊆r⁡{0,e1,e2,e1+e2}.F-b_{F}\subseteq r\{0,e_{1},e_{2},e_{1}+e_{2}\}.

If |F|=4|F|=4, then

A=(bF+[0,r]​e1+[0,r]​e2)∩L,A=\bigl(b_{F}+[0,r]e_{1}+[0,r]e_{2}\bigr)\cap L,

and hence

Nr​(A)r2=Ns​(A)s2=1.\frac{N_{r}(A)}{r^{2}}=\frac{N_{s}(A)}{s^{2}}=1.
Proof.

Only the four-point assertion needs proof. The four corners force the parallelogram bF+[0,r]​e1+[0,r]​e2b_{F}+[0,r]e_{1}+[0,r]e_{2} into PP. It contains (r+1)2=s2(r+1)^{2}=s^{2} lattice points. Injectivity modulo s​LsL gives |A|≤s2|A|\leq s^{2}, so these are all the points of AA, and they represent all r2r^{2} classes modulo r​LrL. ∎

4. Lattice segments and their intersections

Fix r≥3r\geq 3 and s=r+1s=r+1. By Lemmas 3.1 and 2.2, we may work with a two-dimensional lattice polygon PP in a rank-two lattice LL such that A=P∩LA=P\cap L is injective modulo s​LsL. We use the basis e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} of Corollary 3.3 and assume that no four-point fiber modulo r​LrL occurs, since that corollary already settles the comparison in this case. By (3.2),

(4.1) t=∑ξ∈L/r​LA∩ξ≠∅(|A∩ξ|−1).t=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\xi\in L/rL\\ A\cap\xi\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}(|A\cap\xi|-1).

From each two-point fiber, select the segment joining its points. From each three-point fiber, select the joining segment parallel to e1e_{1} and the one parallel to e2e_{2}. A singleton contributes no segment. Thus a fiber FF contributes |F|−1|F|-1 segments, at most two, giving exactly tt segments in total. Each selected segment has the form

(4.2) Q=[x,x+r​v]⊆P,Q∩L={x,x+v,…,x+r​v}⊆A.Q=[x,x+rv]\subseteq P,\qquad Q\cap L=\{x,x+v,\ldots,x+rv\}\subseteq A.

Here vv is primitive and, up to sign, is one of

(4.3) e1,e2,e1+e2,e1−e2.e_{1},\qquad e_{2},\qquad e_{1}+e_{2},\qquad e_{1}-e_{2}.

Selected diagonal segments arise only from two-point fibers.

The image of Q∩LQ\cap L modulo r​LrL is the line

(4.4) ℓr(Q):={x+jv+rL:j=0,…,r−1}⊆L/rL.\ell_{r}(Q):=\{x+jv+rL:j=0,\ldots,r-1\}\subseteq L/rL.

Since a primitive vector extends to a basis of LL, it has order rr in L/r​LL/rL. Thus QQ contains r+1r+1 lattice points, whereas ℓr​(Q)\ell_{r}(Q) has rr points.

The next two configurations give Nr​(A)=r2N_{r}(A)=r^{2}. The desired comparison then follows from Ns​(A)=|A|≤s2N_{s}(A)=|A|\leq s^{2}.

Lemma 4.1 (Repeated images of parallel segments).

Suppose that two distinct parallel selected segments Q,Q′Q,Q^{\prime} have the same image modulo r​LrL. Then Nr​(A)=r2N_{r}(A)=r^{2}.

Proof.

Choose a basis in which the segment direction is horizontal. The segments cannot lie on the same line, since their convex hull would have lattice length at least r+1=sr+1=s. Thus their horizontal levels are distinct. Equality of their images modulo r​LrL means that these levels differ by m​rmr for some integer m≥1m\geq 1.

By convexity, conv⁡(Q∪Q′)⊆P\conv(Q\cup Q^{\prime})\subseteq P. This convex hull has a horizontal section of length rr, measured in the chosen lattice coordinates, at every intermediate integer level. Since m​r≥rmr\geq r, we can choose rr consecutive integer levels on or between the two lines. They give all vertical residues modulo rr, and every horizontal section of length rr contains at least rr consecutive lattice points. Thus every horizontal residue also occurs. All lattice points just counted belong to A=P∩LA=P\cap L; hence all r2r^{2} classes are represented. ∎

Lemma 4.2 (Determinant-two directions).

Let r≥3r\geq 3 be an integer, let LL be a rank-two lattice, and let PP be a lattice polygon such that A=P∩LA=P\cap L is injective modulo (r+1)​L(r+1)L. If PP contains two segments of lattice length rr in primitive directions u,vu,v whose determinant in a basis of LL has absolute value two, then Nr​(A)=r2N_{r}(A)=r^{2}.

Proof.

Injectivity modulo (r+1)​L(r+1)L forbids a segment of lattice length r+1r+1 in PP. The classes of u,vu,v modulo 2​L2L are nonzero and linearly dependent, so u≡v(mod2​L)u\equiv v\pmod{2L}. Consequently, (u+v)/2(u+v)/2 and (u−v)/2(u-v)/2 belong to LL and have determinant of absolute value one, hence form a basis of LL. In these coordinates, after translation, the two segments are

[(0,0),(r,r)],[(a,r+c),(a+r,c)],a,c∈ℤ.[(0,0),(r,r)],\qquad[(a,r+c),(a+r,c)],\qquad a,c\in\mathbb{Z}.

Interchanging the coordinates swaps a,ca,c. Interchanging the segments and applying (x,y)↦(x−a,r+c−y)(x,y)\mapsto(x-a,r+c-y) replaces (a,c)(a,c) by (−a,c)(-a,c). These operations allow us to assume a≥c≥0a\geq c\geq 0.

By convexity, PP contains the triangle with vertices (0,0),(a,r+c),(a+r,c)(0,0),(a,r+c),(a+r,c). Its intersection with y=cy=c contains

[a​cr+c,a+r]×{c}.\left[\frac{ac}{r+c},\,a+r\right]\times\{c\}.

The absence of a segment of lattice length r+1r+1 therefore gives

a+r−⌈a​cr+c⌉≤r,hencea​r<r+c≤r+a.a+r-\left\lceil\frac{ac}{r+c}\right\rceil\leq r,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad ar<r+c\leq r+a.

Thus (r−1)​a<r(r-1)a<r, so a≤1a\leq 1. If a=1a=1, the strict inequality forces c=1c=1. Consequently (a,c)(a,c) is either (0,0)(0,0) or (1,1)(1,1).

In the first case, the convex hull of the two segments is [0,r]2[0,r]^{2}. In the second, (1,1),(r,r)(1,1),(r,r) lie on the first segment, and joining (1,1)(1,1) to the endpoints of the second gives (r,1),(1,r)∈P(r,1),(1,r)\in P. Hence [1,r]2⊆P[1,r]^{2}\subseteq P in both cases. Its r2r^{2} lattice points represent every class modulo r​LrL, proving Nr​(A)=r2N_{r}(A)=r^{2}. ∎

Two primitive directions are unimodular if they form a basis of LL. Outside the two cases above, the direction classes are pairwise unimodular: among (4.3), only the two diagonals have determinant of absolute value two. Thus at most three direction classes remain.

Lemma 4.3 (Intersections and concurrence).

Two selected segments whose directions form a basis of LL meet in a lattice point. Moreover, if three selected segments have pairwise-unimodular directions and their images modulo r​LrL have a common point, then the three segments meet at one lattice point.

Proof.

Modulo s​LsL, a primitive vector has order ss, so the reduction of Q∩LQ\cap L is a complete affine line of ss points. The two affine lines in these basis directions meet in exactly one class modulo s​LsL. Each of the two segments contains a representative of that class, and injectivity modulo s​LsL forces the two representatives to coincide.

For the second assertion, let pi​jp_{ij} be the intersection of the iith and jjth segments. Pairwise unimodularity implies that all pi​jp_{ij} lie in the common class modulo r​LrL. If they are not all equal, they are pairwise distinct: equality of two puts one point on all three segments. On each segment, write the difference of its two intersection points as k​uku, where uu is its primitive direction and 0<|k|≤r0<|k|\leq r. Their congruence modulo r​LrL gives k​u∈r​Lku\in rL. Since uu extends to a basis of LL, this forces r|kr\mid k, so |k|=r|k|=r and the intersection points are the two endpoints. All three segments would therefore have their endpoints in one r​LrL-fiber, whereas at most two segments were selected from any fiber. ∎

5. Covering and counting on the finite torus

For the geometric argument below, let r≥3r\geq 3 be an integer. Sections 3 and 4 handle four-point fibers, parallel segments with the same image modulo r​LrL, and determinant-two pairs: each forces all classes modulo r​LrL to be represented. In the remaining case, the selected segments have distinct images modulo r​LrL and pairwise-unimodular direction classes. The two diagonal directions in (4.3) cannot both occur. Replacing e2e_{2} by −e2-e_{2} if necessary, we may assume that the occurring directions are among

e1,e2,e1+e2,e_{1},\qquad e_{2},\qquad e_{1}+e_{2},

up to sign. Identify LL with ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} and linℝ⁡L\lin_{\mathbb{R}}L with ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} using the basis e1,e2e_{1},e_{2}. We use these coordinates both for the segments and for their residue classes. Thus L/r​LL/rL is identified with

Gr:=(ℤ/r​ℤ)2.G_{r}:=(\mathbb{Z}/r\mathbb{Z})^{2}.

Write ℋ,𝒱,𝒟\mathcal{H},\mathcal{V},\mathcal{D} for the three families of lines in GrG_{r} given respectively by

y=a,x=b,x−y=c(a,b,c∈ℤ/rℤ).y=a,\qquad x=b,\qquad x-y=c\qquad(a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}/r\mathbb{Z}).

Each family contains rr disjoint lines of rr points, and every point lies on one line from each class. If 𝒮⊆ℋ∪𝒱∪𝒟\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{H}\cup\mathcal{V}\cup\mathcal{D}, put

U⁡(𝒮):=⋃ℓ∈𝒮ℓ.U(\mathcal{S}):=\bigcup_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}}\ell.

The transformations

(x,y)⟼(y,x),(x,y)⟼(x,x−y)(x,y)\longmapsto(y,x),\qquad(x,y)\longmapsto(x,x-y)

generate every permutation of the three unoriented direction classes, up to a sign change of a line parameter. These integer linear maps preserve lattice lengths, congruences, and intersections.

The main geometric step is to complete the images of the selected segments to a cover with 2​r+12r+1 lines. The construction uses the intersection and concurrence properties established in Lemma 4.3.

Proposition 5.1 (Completion to a cover).

Let r≥3r\geq 3 be an integer, and let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be a family of segments selected as in Section 4. Suppose that it uses at most three direction classes and that every pair of distinct classes is unimodular. Put

𝒮:={ℓr​(Q):Q∈𝒬}.\mathcal{S}:=\{\ell_{r}(Q):Q\in\mathcal{Q}\}.

Assume that distinct parallel segments have distinct images modulo r​LrL. Then there is a family 𝒞\mathcal{C} of exactly 2​r+12r+1 distinct lines from a pairwise-unimodular triple extending the direction classes occurring in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} such that

𝒮⊆𝒞,U⁡(𝒞)=Gr.\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{C},\qquad U(\mathcal{C})=G_{r}.
Proof.

If fewer than three direction classes occur, extend them to a pairwise-unimodular triple; this fixes three ambient classes but adds no selected line. Use the common lattice coordinates described above. Let u,v,wu,v,w be the numbers of selected horizontal, vertical, and diagonal lines, respectively; some of these numbers may be zero. If, say, u+v≤r+1u+v\leq r+1, include all rr lines of the third class and add r+1−u−vr+1-u-v unused lines from the first two classes. There are 2​r−u−v2r-u-v such unused lines, so this gives a cover with exactly 2​r+12r+1 lines.

We may therefore suppose that every pairwise sum among u,v,wu,v,w is at least r+2r+2. In particular, all three selected families are nonempty. Let Y,X,W⊆ℤY,X,W\subseteq\mathbb{Z} be the integer parameters of the lines containing the selected segments: y∈Yy\in Y, x∈Xx\in X, and x−y∈Wx-y\in W, respectively. These are their parameters in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, before reduction modulo rr. Put

a=max⁡Y−min⁡Y,b=max⁡X−min⁡X,c=max⁡W−min⁡W.a=\max Y-\min Y,\qquad b=\max X-\min X,\qquad c=\max W-\min W.

Each span is at most rr. For example, any selected vertical segment meets the selected horizontal segments at the smallest and largest parameters by Lemma 4.3, and both intersection points lie on that segment of lattice length rr. Equality would give two parallel segments with the same image modulo r​LrL, so

(5.1) a,b,c≤r−1.a,b,c\leq r-1.

Since an integer parameter set of size uu has span at least u−1u-1, the pairwise-sum assumption gives

(5.2) a+b≥r,a+c≥r,b+c≥r.a+b\geq r,\qquad a+c\geq r,\qquad b+c\geq r.

Use the three-class symmetry to make aa the smallest span. Apply the translation (x,y)↦(x−min⁡Y−min⁡W,y−min⁡Y)(x,y)\mapsto(x-\min Y-\min W,y-\min Y). Denote the translated parameter sets again by Y,X,WY,X,W and put d=min⁡Xd=\min X. Then

(5.3) Y⊆[0,a],X⊆[d,d+b],W⊆[0,c].Y\subseteq[0,a],\qquad X\subseteq[d,d+b],\qquad W\subseteq[0,c].

Here and below, intervals denote sets of integers; their residues index torus lines. An interval with upper endpoint below its lower endpoint is empty.

If d>cd>c, the selected horizontal segment at level 00 contains its intersections with the lines x−y=0x-y=0 and x=d+bx=d+b, and therefore d+b≤rd+b\leq r. Together with a+b≥ra+b\geq r, this gives d≤a≤cd\leq a\leq c, a contradiction. If d<a−bd<a-b, the selected horizontal segment at level aa contains its intersections with x=dx=d and x−y=cx-y=c, so a+c−d≤ra+c-d\leq r; the inequality b+c≥rb+c\geq r then yields d≥a−bd\geq a-b, again a contradiction. Hence

(5.4) a−b≤d≤c.a-b\leq d\leq c.

If d≥0d\geq 0, apply (x,y)↦(x,x−y)(x,y)\mapsto(x,x-y). The new parameter sets are

Y′=W,X′=X,W′=Y.Y^{\prime}=W,\qquad X^{\prime}=X,\qquad W^{\prime}=Y.

If d<0d<0, apply (x,y)↦(−y,−x)(x,y)\mapsto(-y,-x) and translate both coordinates by d+bd+b. Then

Y′⊆[0,b],X′⊆[d+b−a,d+b],W′⊆[0,c].Y^{\prime}\subseteq[0,b],\quad X^{\prime}\subseteq[d+b-a,d+b],\quad W^{\prime}\subseteq[0,c].

Their images modulo r​LrL concur, but the segments do not, contradicting Lemma 4.3. If a+c−d=ra+c-d=r, use the selected segments on y=ay=a, x=dx=d, and x−y=cx-y=c: their pairwise intersections are (d,a),(a+c,a),(d,d−c)(d,a),(a+c,a),(d,d-c), and the same contradiction applies. (5.7) d+b≤r−1,a+c−d≤r−1.d+b\leq r-1,\qquad a+c-d\leq r-1.

x−y(modr)∈[1,r+d−a−2]⊆W∗.x-y\pmod{r}\in[1,r+d-a-2]\subseteq W^{*}.

When one of these displayed intervals is empty, the implication is vacuous. The corresponding torus lines form the required 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Pulling them back through the affine-unimodular normalizations completes the proof. ∎

It remains to estimate how many points the selected lines cover. The next lemma applies to every subfamily of a cover of the size just constructed.

Lemma 5.2 (Counting in a cover).

Let r≥3r\geq 3, and let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a cover of GrG_{r} by exactly 2​r+12r+1 distinct lines from ℋ∪𝒱∪𝒟\mathcal{H}\cup\mathcal{V}\cup\mathcal{D}. For every 𝒮⊆𝒞\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{C},

(5.9) |U⁡(𝒮)|≥r2​|𝒮|2​r+1.|U(\mathcal{S})|\geq\frac{r^{2}|\mathcal{S}|}{2r+1}.
Proof.

Put m=|𝒮|m=|\mathcal{S}|, and let u,v,wu,v,w be its three direction counts. If m≤3​r/2m\leq 3r/2, inclusion–exclusion gives

|U⁡(𝒮)|≥r​m−(u​v+u​w+v​w)≥r​m−m23≥r​m2≥r2​m2​r+1.|U(\mathcal{S})|\geq rm-(uv+uw+vw)\geq rm-\frac{m^{2}}{3}\geq\frac{rm}{2}\geq\frac{r^{2}m}{2r+1}.

Suppose that m>3​r/2m>3r/2, and put M=⌊(r−1)/2⌋M=\lfloor(r-1)/2\rfloor. We restore the lines of 𝒞∖𝒮\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{S} one at a time. a+b+c=3​r−|𝒯|<3​r2.a+b+c=3r-|\mathcal{T}|<\frac{3r}{2}.

If all remaining lines have one direction, the missing lines in the other two classes lie outside 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Their total number is at most 3​r−(2​r+1)=r−13r-(2r+1)=r-1, so a remaining line covers at most MM new points. Otherwise, if every remaining line covered at least M+1M+1 new points, the bounds from two different directions would imply a,b,c≥M+1a,b,c\geq M+1. This contradicts

a+b+c<3​r2≤3​(M+1).a+b+c<\frac{3r}{2}\leq 3(M+1).

r2−|U⁡(𝒮)|≤(2​r+1−m)​M≤r2​(2​r+1−m)2​r+1,r^{2}-|U(\mathcal{S})|\leq(2r+1-m)M\leq\frac{r^{2}(2r+1-m)}{2r+1},

where M≤(r−1)/2<r2/(2​r+1)M\leq(r-1)/2<r^{2}/(2r+1). Rearranging proves the claim. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

By Section 2, it suffices to compare moduli rr and s=r+1s=r+1 for r≥3r\geq 3 and a nonempty finite lattice-convex set AA in a rank-two lattice LL. By Lemma 3.1, we may assume that reduction modulo s​LsL is injective on AA. If AA has affine dimension at most one, use Lemma 2.2. Otherwise put P=conv⁡(A)P=\conv(A) and t=|A|−Nr​(A)t=|A|-N_{r}(A). Since Ns​(A)=|A|N_{s}(A)=|A|, the desired comparison is equivalent to

(5.10) Nr​(A)≥r2​t2​r+1.N_{r}(A)\geq\frac{r^{2}t}{2r+1}.

If Nr​(A)=r2N_{r}(A)=r^{2}, the comparison follows directly from Ns​(A)=|A|≤s2N_{s}(A)=|A|\leq s^{2}. We may therefore assume Nr​(A)<r2N_{r}(A)<r^{2}.

Use the coordinates of Corollary 3.3. No fiber has four points, since that would give Nr​(A)=r2N_{r}(A)=r^{2}. Select tt segments as in Section 4. Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2 exclude equal images of parallel segments and determinant-two pairs. Thus the selected direction classes are pairwise unimodular. Images in different classes are also distinct, since they meet in exactly one point and each has r>1r>1 points. Their family 𝒮\mathcal{S} therefore has tt lines.

Proposition 5.1 gives a cover with 2​r+12r+1 lines containing 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Lemma 5.2 gives

Nr​(A)≥|U⁡(𝒮)|≥r2​t2​r+1,N_{r}(A)\geq|U(\mathcal{S})|\geq\frac{r^{2}t}{2r+1},

where the first inequality holds because every lattice point on a selected segment belongs to AA. This proves (5.10).

Lemma 3.1 transfers the comparison to the original set. Chaining consecutive comparisons and then summing over the affine cosets in (2.2) proves the theorem. ∎

Remark 5.3.

In Lemma 5.2, the last comparison in each case is strict when ∅≠𝒮⊊𝒞\varnothing\neq\mathcal{S}\subsetneq\mathcal{C}. Hence equality in (5.9) holds precisely for 𝒮=∅\mathcal{S}=\varnothing or 𝒮=𝒞\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{C}.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.1, put i=rank⁡Γi=\rank\Gamma and c=DΛ​(K,Γ)c=D_{\Lambda}(K,\Gamma). For integers 1≤r<s1\leq r<s,

DΛ​(K,r​Γ)ri=DΛ​(K,s​Γ)si⟺DΛ(K,sΓ)=sic.\frac{D_{\Lambda}(K,r\Gamma)}{r^{i}}=\frac{D_{\Lambda}(K,s\Gamma)}{s^{i}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_{\Lambda}(K,s\Gamma)=s^{i}c.

Thus equal values occur only at the maximum cc; once the normalized counts fall below cc, they decrease strictly.

If c=0c=0 or i=0i=0, the assertion is immediate. Otherwise, Lemma 2.1 expresses the difference of the normalized counts as a sum of nonnegative differences over the nonempty slices AξA_{\xi}. Equality forces equality on every slice, and monotonicity then gives

si​Ns−1​(Aξ,Γ)=(s−1)i​Ns​(Aξ,Γ).s^{i}N_{s-1}(A_{\xi};\Gamma)=(s-1)^{i}N_{s}(A_{\xi};\Gamma).

Since gcd⁡(si,(s−1)i)=1\gcd(s^{i},(s-1)^{i})=1 and 1≤Ns​(Aξ,Γ)≤si1\leq N_{s}(A_{\xi};\Gamma)\leq s^{i}, we obtain Ns​(Aξ,Γ)=siN_{s}(A_{\xi};\Gamma)=s^{i}. Summing over the cc nonempty slices proves the forward implication. Conversely, monotonicity and the value cc at modulus one give c≥DΛ​(K,r​Γ)/ri≥DΛ​(K,s​Γ)/si=cc\geq D_{\Lambda}(K,r\Gamma)/r^{i}\geq D_{\Lambda}(K,s\Gamma)/s^{i}=c.
